youtube.hook: There are thousands of programming languages — but only about a dozen actually run the world. Every app, every website, every game, every AI is built in one of them. And they're not random: each was born to fix a pain in the one before it.

segments.narration: There are thousands of programming languages in existence — but only about a dozen actually run the world. Every app, every website, every game, every A-I, is built in one of them. And they are not random: each one was born to solve a specific pain in the language before it — so together, they form a kind of family tree. So let's walk that tree. Here is every programming language that truly matters — what it's for, what makes it special, and why it exists at all — told one Hello World at a time.

segments.name: C
segments.narration: C is the bedrock that everything else stands on. Written in nineteen-seventy-two to build Unix, it gives you direct, almost physical control over the computer's memory — which makes it blisteringly fast, and famously unforgiving. Your operating system, your database, even most of the other languages on this very list, are written in C. Fifty years on, nothing has truly replaced it.
segments.verdict: The bedrock — direct, fast, unforgiving; it's still under everything.

segments.name: C++
segments.narration: C-plus-plus took C and added objects — a way to model complex things — while keeping every bit of C's raw speed. It is enormous and intricate, handing you total control, and plenty of rope to hang yourself with. It is the language of triple-A games, web browsers, and high-frequency trading: anywhere you need maximum performance, but with real structure.
segments.verdict: C with objects — maximum performance and maximum complexity.

segments.name: Python
segments.narration: Python made a radical bet: that programmer time matters more than computer time. Its code reads almost like plain English, so it is the easiest of the big languages to learn — and it is now the single most popular language on Earth. It is a little slow, but it is the undisputed king of data science, machine learning and A-I. If you only ever learn one language, learn this one.
segments.verdict: The everyman — easiest to learn, and the king of AI and data.

segments.name: Ruby
segments.narration: Ruby was designed around one single goal: making the programmer happy. It is elegant and expressive, optimised for how humans think, not how machines work. It exploded thanks to Rails — the framework that let tiny teams build entire web startups astonishingly fast. Twitter, GitHub and Shopify all began their lives written in Ruby.
segments.verdict: Built for joy — elegant, expressive, and the heart of Rails.

segments.name: Java
segments.narration: Java's promise was 'write once, run anywhere': your code runs on a virtual machine, so it simply does not care what computer it lands on. That made it the default language of big, serious systems — banks, massive backends, and every Android app. It is verbose and ceremonial, but incredibly stable. Billions of devices quietly run Java right now.
segments.verdict: Write once, run anywhere — the stable backbone of enterprise and Android.

segments.name: JavaScript
segments.narration: JavaScript was famously built in just ten days — and then accidentally took over the world. It is the only language that runs natively inside every web browser, which makes it completely unavoidable: every interactive website you have ever used runs on it. It then escaped the browser to run servers too. It is quirky, chaotic, and utterly, totally dominant.

specs.label: Superpower
specs.value: the only language in the browser

segments.verdict: Born in 10 days — the one language every browser speaks.

segments.name: PHP
segments.narration: P-H-P is the unglamorous workhorse that quietly built the web. It was designed for exactly one thing — generating web pages on a server — and it did it so simply that an enormous share of all websites, including the early Facebook and most of WordPress, still run on it today. Everyone loves to mock P-H-P. It is also, still, absolutely everywhere.
segments.verdict: The mocked workhorse — still quietly running a huge slice of the web.

segments.name: C#
segments.narration: C-sharp was Microsoft's answer to Java — and it grew into one of the most polished, genuinely pleasant languages to write. It runs the Windows software world, and crucially, it is the language of Unity, the engine behind a huge portion of the games you actually play. Modern, fast, and beautifully tooled from top to bottom.
segments.verdict: Microsoft's polished all-rounder — and the language of Unity games.

segments.name: Go
segments.narration: Go was built at Google by people utterly fed up with complexity. Its entire philosophy is ruthless simplicity: a small language you can genuinely learn in a weekend, with brilliant built-in support for doing thousands of things at once. That made it the language of the modern cloud — Docker and Kubernetes are both written in Go.
segments.verdict: Ruthless simplicity + easy concurrency — the language of the cloud.

segments.name: Rust
segments.narration: Rust solves a problem that haunted C for fifty years: memory bugs, the root cause of most serious security holes. Its clever 'borrow checker' guarantees memory safety at compile time — with zero runtime cost, so it stays as fast as C. It is famously hard to learn, and, for years running now, it is the language developers most adore.
segments.verdict: C's speed with guaranteed memory safety — and the most loved language.

segments.name: TypeScript
segments.narration: TypeScript is JavaScript, but with a safety net. It adds a type system on top of J-S — catching a whole class of silly, costly bugs before your code ever runs — then compiles straight back down to plain JavaScript. It has quietly become the default for serious web projects: most large front-ends today are written in TypeScript, not raw J-S.
segments.verdict: JavaScript with a type safety net — now the default for big web apps.

segments.name: Swift
segments.narration: Swift is Apple's modern language, built to replace the ageing Objective-C. It is clean, safe and fast — and it is how essentially every new iPhone, iPad and Mac app is written today. If you want to build for Apple's billion-plus devices, this is simply the language you reach for. Easy to read, hard to misuse.
segments.verdict: Apple's clean, safe modern language — how iOS & Mac apps are built.

segments.narration: Step back, and the whole family sorts neatly onto one spectrum. At one end: the compiled, close-to-the-metal languages — C, C-plus-plus, Rust — that talk almost directly to the hardware. Brutally fast, but demanding. At the other end: the interpreted, human-friendly ones — Python, JavaScript, Ruby — that happily trade raw speed for the sheer joy of getting things done. There is no single 'best' language. There is only the right tool for the job, and the trade-off you are willing to make.

segments.question: What was your first language?
segments.narration: So that is the family: a dozen languages, each one solving the pain of the one before it. C for raw power, Python for ease, JavaScript for the web, Rust for safety — all different answers to the same question of how we talk to machines. And the secret nobody tells beginners? Once you truly learn one of them, the next comes easy; they are all just variations on the same few ideas.
